### Scope and Intent

The Project Tick General Public License is a copyleft license intended for software programs. It is designed to preserve the core freedoms defined by the Open Source Definition while addressing a specific and well-documented gap in contemporary software deployment models: network-based operation without traditional distribution.

Unlike existing licenses that either do not address network operation at all, or that apply network-based obligations in a broad and unconditional manner, this license introduces a narrowly scoped and copyright-holder-controlled mechanism for treating certain network-based operation as conveying solely for the purpose of source availability.

The license explicitly avoids discrimination against persons, groups, or fields of endeavor, and imposes no usage-based or purpose-based restrictions.

### Open Source Definition Compatibility

The license is designed to comply fully with the Open Source Definition, including but not limited to:

- OSD §3 (Derived Works): Modified versions and derivative works are explicitly permitted and must remain under the same license.
- OSD §5 (No Discrimination Against Persons or Groups): No restrictions are imposed based on identity, affiliation, or status.
- OSD §6 (No Discrimination Against Fields of Endeavor): The license permits use for all purposes, including commercial use.
- OSD §9 (License Must Not Be Specific to a Product): The license applies generically to software programs and is not tied to any specific product or platform.

### Rationale for a New License

This license does not seek to replace existing OSI-approved copyleft licenses. Instead, it formalizes a distinct behavioral model that is not fully captured by existing licenses, particularly with respect to narrowly defined, opt-in treatment of network-based operation and equal access to corresponding source resources.

The intent is to prevent models in which source code is made available only to contractual counterparties or paying customers, while excluding the broader user community that meaningfully interacts with the software.

Hi Duman-san,

Thank you for submitting the Project Tick General Public License v2.0.
Since this text was first introduced on license-discuss as a draft, I would
prefer we continue the substantive design discussion there first, and
return to license-review once the open points are resolved with a
review-friendly package.

Two items from license-discuss still look open:

* GPL text derivation and a focused diff
Bruce Perens raised concerns about substantial derivation from GPL text and
asked for a clearer presentation of what is actually new. Before a full OSD
review, it would help to provide either a redline against GPLv3/AGPLv3 or a
short “innovations only” excerpt, along with a brief explanation of why
existing OSI-approved licenses plus additional permissions/exceptions or
guidance cannot achieve the same goals.

* “Explicit Network Use Notice” consistency
David Woolley questioned whether the “Explicit Network Use Notice”
structure effectively creates two licenses and suggested clarifying the
mechanism so the trigger conditions cannot be misunderstood. The submission
rationale emphasizes an opt-in design, so it would be helpful to make the
trigger and consequences unambiguous and consistent across the text.

As a minor flag (not a full analysis here), v2.0 still includes strong
“publicly available” requirements and access-modality constraints (for
example, around account registration and acceptance of inconsistent terms).
Even if the policy goal is clear, it may be worth the submitter explaining
how these are intended to fit under OSD #10’s technology neutrality and
“style of interface” language.

If the submitter can address the two license-discuss points above and
provide the requested diff/excerpt, I think the subsequent license-review
discussion will be much more efficient.

1. GPL text derivation and scope of novelty

The Project Tick General Public License v2.0 intentionally reuses GPL-style structure, terminology, and ordering. This is a deliberate design choice aimed at legal familiarity and predictability, not an assertion of originality of expression.
